\begin{document}

\title{Self-Hosted LLMs for Accessible Software Engineering:\\
A Drift-, Bias- and Cost-Aware Evaluation on an 8\,GB Consumer GPU}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Anonymous Author(s)}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Affiliation withheld for review}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Large language models (LLMs) now write and repair user-interface code, yet comparisons of
LLMs rarely measure accessibility, usually test one-shot prompts, sometimes let a model judge
its own output, and seldom report cost. We present an evaluation framework that measures
accessible software engineering as it happens in practice. Six capability dimensions anchored in
WCAG~2.2 are scored by real-browser oracles (axe-core and \res{probe-count} keyboard and
semantics probes). The \emph{Dynamic Contextual Drift Index} (DCDI) measures how much
accessibility adherence an agent loses over a long, tool-using session, against a fresh-context
control and a length-matched padded control. \emph{Cross-Model Blind Peer Evaluation} (CMBPE)
is an anonymised, family-recused, order-permuted and length-adjusted jury for alt text,
calibrated against ratings by blind and low-vision people. \emph{Capability-per-Dollar-Second}
(CPDS) relates capability to cost and latency with bootstrap Pareto membership. We apply the
framework to four open-weight models that a small organisation can self-host for free on one
8\,GB consumer GPU (\Q, \QV, \GM{} and \MI, 4-bit), with \res{total-calls-answered} answered model
calls on \res{run-dates}.
%FINDINGS-ABSTRACT
Every reported value is computed by committed code from logged responses; code, prompts,
logs and scores are public.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
accessibility, WCAG 2.2, large language models, LLM-as-a-judge, agents, evaluation, alt text
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% ======================================================================================
\section{Introduction}

Most web pages still fail automated accessibility checks, and code assistants now write a
growing share of user-interface code. Whether that code is accessible therefore matters for
blind, low-vision, motor-impaired and keyboard-only users. Studies of LLMs and accessibility
report that generated code often misses accessibility requirements unless they are requested,
and that models can fix many violations once they are pointed out
\cite{aljedaani2024chatgpt,mowar2025codea11y}. These studies usually test one or two models
with one-shot prompts, judge outputs with a single (sometimes the same) model, and do not report
what an evaluation or a remediation costs.

Four practical questions remain open. Does a model build accessible interfaces
\emph{by default}, or only when told to? Does it keep honouring accessibility while it works
through a long, tool-using session, where its context fills with history
\cite{liu2024lost,hsieh2024ruler}? Can LLM judges rate accessibility content such as alt text
reliably, given their known position, length and self-preference biases
\cite{zheng2023judging,wang2024fair,panickssery2024self}? And what does AI-assisted remediation
cost per page, in money and in time?

We answer these questions with a framework built around automated, browser-based oracles and
three new measures (DCDI, CMBPE and CPDS), and we apply it to the setting most relevant to
organisations without an API budget: small open-weight models served locally on one 8\,GB
consumer GPU. Our research questions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{RQ1} How do the models perform across six accessibility-engineering capability
  dimensions (C1--C6)?
\item \textbf{RQ2} Do LLM agents keep honouring accessibility requirements as a long,
  tool-using session grows?
\item \textbf{RQ3} Does a blind, family-recused, order-permuted, length-adjusted jury (CMBPE)
  judge accessibility content more reliably than single LLM judges?
\item \textbf{RQ4} Which models are Pareto-efficient in capability, cost and latency, and what
  does AI-assisted remediation cost?
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Contributions.} (1) A capability taxonomy that maps general LLM abilities to six
WCAG~2.2-anchored tasks with automated oracles, including \res{probe-count} keyboard and
semantics probes, each validated on a passing and a failing fixture. (2) DCDI, a drift
measure with a counterfactual fresh-context control and a padded control that separates the
effect of context length from the effect of the session's history. (3) CMBPE, a bias-controlled
jury with a Bradley--Terry model of position and length bias. (4) CPDS, a scenario-weighted
efficiency score with bootstrap Pareto membership. (5) A fully logged study of four self-hosted
models, with code, prompts, raw scores and call logs released.

\textbf{Scope.} This study evaluates 4--8B open-weight models at 4-bit quantisation, served by
llama.cpp \cite{llamacpp} on one consumer GPU. It does not evaluate frontier closed models.
The harness supports them, but running them needs paid API access. Claims about the
frontier, or about closed versus open models, are therefore out of scope here.

% ======================================================================================
\section{Related Work}

\textbf{LLMs and accessible code.} Aljedaani et al.\ studied the accessibility of web code
generated by ChatGPT and its ability to repair violations \cite{aljedaani2024chatgpt}.
CodeA11y adds accessibility-aware suggestions and reminders to an AI coding assistant and
evaluates them with developers \cite{mowar2025codea11y}. We complement such studies with
repeated, multi-model measurement, a repair corpus with known faults, long agentic sessions and
cost.

\textbf{Automated accessibility testing.} Rule engines such as axe-core \cite{axecore} check a
subset of WCAG success criteria \cite{wcag22} in a rendered page; keyboard operability, focus
management and widget state largely escape them. We pair axe-core with browser-driven probes
(Playwright \cite{playwright}) and treat all automated results as lower bounds on failures.

\textbf{LLM-as-a-judge.} LLM judges favour the first-shown or longer answer and their own
outputs \cite{zheng2023judging,wang2024fair,panickssery2024self}. CMBPE combines several known
mitigations (both orders, anonymisation, recusal) with an explicit Bradley--Terry model
\cite{bradley1952rank} of position and length bias, and calibrates the jury against human
ratings.

\textbf{Long contexts and agents.} Models use information in long contexts unevenly
\cite{liu2024lost}, and effective context is often shorter than the advertised window
\cite{hsieh2024ruler}. Agentic coding benchmarks measure task success \cite{jimenez2024swebench}
but not whether non-functional requirements stated once at the start are still honoured many
steps later. DCDI measures exactly that.

\textbf{Alt-text evaluation.} Kreiss et al.\ showed that context matters for the usefulness
of image descriptions to blind and low-vision (BLV) readers and collected BLV ratings
\cite{kreiss2022context}. ContextRef provides crowd ratings of descriptions in Wikipedia
context \cite{kreiss2024contextref}. We use both as calibration data for LLM judges.

% ======================================================================================
\section{Framework}

\subsection{Oracles and the rule-level pass rate}
Pages are rendered in headless Chromium \res{chromium-version} at 1280$\times$800 and served from
a local HTTP server that blocks every other host. axe-core \res{axe-version} runs with the WCAG
2.x Level A and AA rule tags. Pages with timers are checked again after 6\,s, and a rule fails
if it failed in either run. \res{probe-count} probes cover what axe cannot see. Three generic
probes run on every page: tab reachability, visible focus and no keyboard trap. The others
cover widget patterns: form errors associated with their fields and not shown by colour
alone, dialog focus handling, tabs, accordions, disclosure navigation, comboboxes, sliders,
switches, tooltips, live regions, data-table headers, sort controls, pause controls for moving
content, multi-step focus management, captions, landmarks, headings, language of parts,
contrast after a theme toggle and accessible names that are not placeholder-only. Every probe
passes its accessible fixture and fails its inaccessible fixture. Probes find widgets by
visible text anchors, never by implementation details, and accept any keyboard path that
satisfies the success criterion.

For an artefact $x$, let $Q(x)$ be the applicable checks: every axe rule that evaluated at
least one node in scope, plus every applicable probe. The pass rate is
\begin{equation}
a(x) = |\{q\in Q(x) : q \text{ passes}\}| \,/\, |Q(x)| .
\end{equation}
Task-specific functional checks (for example ``an empty submit is blocked'') confirm that the
page does what was asked.

\subsection{Capability taxonomy}
Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy} lists the six dimensions and their scores $S_k\in[0,1]$. The composite
capability score is the weighted geometric mean
$\mathrm{CCS}_m = \exp\big(\sum_k w_k \ln \max(S_{m,k}, 0.01)\big)$ with $w_k = 1/6$, reported
only for models with all six scores; a geometric mean keeps a weak dimension from being
masked by strong ones.

\toprule
Dimension & Experiment & Score \\
\midrule

C2 accessible UI generation and repair & E1-Gen, E1-Repair & $S_2 = (S_\text{gen}+S_\text{rep})/2$\\

C4 text alternatives for images & E3c & $S_4$ = CMBPE expected win rate\\

\subsection{Dynamic Contextual Drift Index (DCDI)}
An agent works through a fixed sequence of steps on one workspace. After each step $t$ of run
$r$ we score the in-session adherence $a_{r,t}$ on the step's scope and checks. A \emph{fresh
control} replays the same step in a new conversation on a copy of the workspace snapshot
$S_{r,t-1}$, with the same system prompt and tool budget, giving $a^0_{r,t}$. Over the
foundation and regular steps $T_\text{reg}$ that are functional in both arms,
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{DCDI}_m = \frac{\sum_{r,t\in T_\text{reg}} (a^0_{r,t} - a_{r,t})}{\sum_{r,t\in T_\text{reg}} a^0_{r,t}} .
\end{equation}
DCDI is 0 without drift, 1 when all adherence is lost and negative when history helps. A
\emph{padded control} at checkpoints $K$ replays the step after irrelevant history whose
length matches the session's prompt length $\Lambda_{r,t}$ within $\pm$10\,\%. It splits the
drift at the checkpoints into a length and a history component,
$\mathrm{DCDI}_K = [\sum (a^0 - a^\text{pad}) + \sum (a^\text{pad} - a)] / \sum a^0 =
\mathrm{DCDI}_\text{len} + \mathrm{DCDI}_\text{hist}$. The drift rate $\beta_m$ is the OLS
slope of $a^0-a$ on $\log_2(\Lambda/8192)$ with step fixed effects (adherence lost per
doubling of context).

\subsection{Cross-Model Blind Peer Evaluation (CMBPE)}
Judges from different model families compare two anonymised candidates for the same image in
both orders. Candidate texts are stripped of quotes, markdown and lead-ins such as ``Image
of'', then given random opaque ids. A verdict is dropped from aggregation when the judge's family
equals either candidate's family (recusal). With $y=1$ if the first-shown candidate wins,
\begin{equation}
P(y=1) = \sigma(\theta_a - \theta_b + \delta_j + \gamma_j\,\Delta\ell),
\end{equation}
where $\Delta\ell$ is the standardised length difference, $\delta_j$ and $\gamma_j$ are judge
$j$'s position and length biases, and $\sum\theta = 0$. The model is fitted by penalised
maximum likelihood (ridge $10^{-3}$ on $\theta$) with image-cluster bootstrap intervals.
A generator's score is its expected win rate $S_4(m) = \mathrm{mean}_{g\neq m}\,\sigma(\theta_m -
\theta_g)$. Self-preference $\eta_j$ is estimated from judge $j$'s own-family verdicts with
$\theta$ fixed at the panel estimate. Position consistency $\mathrm{PC}_j$ is the share of
pairs with the same verdict in both orders. Baselines are a single judge (one seeded order,
no recusal or adjustment), a naive majority panel and a length-only scorer.

\subsection{Capability-per-Dollar-Second (CPDS)}
For model $m$ and task family $f$ (nudged generation, repair), with capability score $CS$,
mean billed cost per task $C$ and median latency $L$,
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{CPDS}^{(\alpha,\beta)} = \frac{CS}{\phi(C/c_0)^{\alpha}\,\phi(L/l_0)^{\beta}},\quad
\phi(z) = 1+\log_{10}(1+z),
\end{equation}
with $c_0 = \$0.01$ and $l_0 = 1$\,s. The scenarios are batch remediation ($\alpha=1,\beta=0$, on
repair), interactive assistant ($\alpha=0.5,\beta=1$, on generation) and balanced
($\alpha=\beta=1$). A model's Pareto-membership probability $\pi_m$ is the share of $B$ bootstrap
resamples in which no other model is at least as capable, cheap and fast and strictly better in
one of them. Self-hosted models have $C = 0$ (electricity is not metered), so CPDS reduces to
a latency-adjusted capability on the stated hardware.

\section{Study Design}

\subsection{Models, hardware and serving}
Table~\ref{tab:models} lists the models. \Q{} \cite{qwen3} is a text model with thinking on by
default; it runs E1 and E2. \QV{} \cite{qwen25vl}, \GM{} \cite{gemma3} and \MI{}
\cite{ministral3} are vision-language models from three families and form the E3 generator
pool and jury; \QV{} also runs E1. All weights are the publishers' Q4\_K\_M GGUF files, pinned
by SHA-256. They are served by llama.cpp b12004 \cite{llamacpp} through its Vulkan backend on
the open Mesa NVK driver, on an NVIDIA RTX~2060~SUPER (8\,GB), an Intel i7-9700K and 32\,GB
RAM (Ubuntu 26.04). Every layer is on the GPU and one model is resident at a time.
\Q{} uses its native 32{,}768-token window with an 8-bit KV cache and may emit up to 32{,}768
tokens, as its model card recommends. The other models may emit up to 8{,}192. The harness
sends no sampling parameters. The server applies each model's Ollama-library defaults (\Q:
temperature 0.6, top-$k$ 20, top-$p$ 0.95; \QV: 0.0001; \GM: 1.0, 64, 0.95; \MI: 0.15), so \QV{} is
close to greedy. Images are encoded with at most 1{,}280 visual tokens (\GM{} uses its fixed
256). A prompt longer than the window is rejected by the server and recorded as context
exhaustion, never truncated. Requests are serialised, so latencies are those of one request
on this machine. Table~\ref{tab:hw} summarises the serving speed and GPU memory measured during
the study (\texttt{experiments/local/extra\_values.py}). The desktop session shares the
GPU, so the memory figures include about 1.3\,GB that the study does not use.

\subsection{E1: generation, repair and audit (C1, C2, C6)}
\textbf{Generation.} 20 interface tasks: form with validation, modal dialog, tabs, accordion,
disclosure navigation, data table, image gallery with lightbox, auto-rotating carousel,
autocomplete combobox, switch, slider, status message, article structure, video, pagination,
tooltip, file upload, multi-step form, consent banner and icon links. Each runs
\emph{unguided} and \emph{nudged} (one added sentence: ``Make sure it is accessible and
conforms to WCAG 2.2 Level AA.''), with 3 samples each. The model must return one
self-contained HTML document; a missing or truncated block scores 0. A second turn asks
whether the page conforms to WCAG~2.2 AA (JSON). $S_\text{gen}$ is the mean over nudged samples
of $a(x)\cdot\mathbb{1}[\text{functional}]$. The \emph{default gap} is $S_\text{gen}$(nudged) $-$
$S_\text{gen}$(unguided). The \emph{overclaim rate} is the share of functional, imperfect pages
($a(x)<1$) that the model claims conform; it is a lower bound, because automated checks miss
failures.

\textbf{Repair.} 12 accessible base pages: 4 adapted W3C ``Before and After'' demonstration
pages \cite{w3cbad} and 8 authored pages. 12 mutation operators inject faults: image alt
removed (SC 1.1.1), label replaced by a placeholder, contrast reduced, icon-button name
removed, icon-link name removed, page language removed, button turned into a \texttt{div},
heading demoted, positive \texttt{tabindex}, focus indicator removed, invalid ARIA attribute
and page title removed. A seeded search yields 48 faulty pages with 4 faults each (192 faults,
16 per operator), and every injected fault is detected by the oracles. A repair scores
$s=\max(0,(\text{resolved}-\text{regressions})/4)\cdot\mathbb{1}[\text{preserved}]$, where
preservation requires visible-text similarity $\geq 0.95$, every base-page id and DOM
tag-sequence similarity $\geq 0.85$. $S_\text{rep}$ is the mean page score.

\textbf{Audit.} The model lists the problems of each faulty page as JSON. Reports are matched
one-to-one to injected faults by success criterion and element. $S_\text{audit}$ is the
micro-F1 over the 192 faults; unmatched reports count as false positives, a lower bound on
precision.

\subsection{E2: long agentic sessions (C3, C5, C6)}
The model builds a small clinic website with three file tools (\texttt{list\_files},
\texttt{read\_file}, \texttt{write\_file}) in a sandboxed workspace. The system prompt states
the WCAG~2.2 AA requirement once; no user message mentions accessibility. There are 24 steps:
4 foundation pages (services, appointments, contact, news), then 14 regular features (hero
banner, site search, accordion, form validation, confirmation dialog, cookie banner, gallery,
language switcher, pagination, back-to-top button, social links, dark-mode switch, news ticker,
pain-level slider) and 6 \emph{pressure} requests that conflict with accessibility
(placeholder-only labels, light-grey footer text, a click-only tile, removing focus outlines,
colour-only validation errors, disabling zoom), in a fixed random order. A step ends when the
model answers without a tool call or after 10 tool calls; history is never truncated or
summarised. Pressure steps score 1 if the model keeps the page accessible, 0.5 for a partial
outcome and 0 if it complies in an inaccessible way. Fresh controls run at every step, padded
controls at positions 8, 12, 16, 20 and 24 (only where the session reaches them), and an
end-of-session audit re-scores every earlier step.

\subsection{E3: alt text and judges (C4)}
D\textsubscript{BLV}: 68 descriptions in article context, each rated by four BLV participants
\cite{kreiss2022context}. D\textsubscript{CR}: 204 descriptions in Wikipedia context with crowd
ratings \cite{kreiss2024contextref}. Images are the datasets' own stimuli (222 distinct images,
all retrieved). The judges, one per family, rate every item on a 5-point scale (pointwise) and
compare pairs in both orders. \emph{E3a} pairs two D\textsubscript{BLV} descriptions of the same
image whose BLV ratings differ by at least 0.5 (23 pairs). \emph{E3b} pairs each original
description with four degraded versions (another item's first sentence appended, repeated text,
another image's description, the first three words), giving 1{,}058 known-answer pairs.
\emph{E3c} has each generator write alt text for 120 seeded D\textsubscript{CR} images. With three
generators all three pairs per image are judged, and after recusal each pair keeps exactly one
judge, from the third family.

\subsection{Statistics}
We report 95\,\% percentile bootstrap intervals ($B=2000$, seed 20271113) that resample the
natural cluster: task (E1-Gen), page (E1-Repair, E1-Audit), run $\times$ step (E2) and image
(E3) \cite{efron1993bootstrap}. All models share the same resamples, so differences are paired.
We call two models different only when the interval of their difference excludes 0.
Hypothesis tests are one-sided bootstrap tests with Holm correction \cite{holm1979simple}.
Inter-judge agreement is Krippendorff's $\alpha$ \cite{krippendorff2004content}.

\subsection{Pre-registered hypotheses and their status in this study}
The framework's pre-registered hypotheses are: H1, larger siblings drift less than smaller ones
(vendor pairs); H2, the best closed model's C4 score exceeds the best open model's; H3, at
least one open-weight model has $\pi\geq 0.5$ on the batch-remediation frontier; H4, (a) some
single judge prefers its own family and (b) CMBPE beats the median single judge on known-answer
pairs; H5, for most models nudged generation beats unguided generation. With four local
open-weight models, H1 and H2 cannot be tested and H3 holds trivially. H4 and H5 are tested as
planned.

\subsection{Changes from the original plan}
The original plan targeted frontier and hosted models through paid APIs. Without an API
budget, this study runs the plan's documented local profile, with these changes (all logged,
dated and motivated in \texttt{experiments/DEVIATIONS.md} before the affected calls):
llama.cpp instead of Ollama, because the latter has no GPU backend on the open driver;
a third local judge family (\MI), without which recusal removes every E3c verdict; a 32{,}768-token
output budget for \Q{} (the plan's rule: the model's maximum output); the image-token cap; the E2
padding transcript written by \Q{} instead of Claude Haiku 5.5, kept to the turns that fit its
window; and one E2 run (seed 101) instead of three. No metric, prompt, task or scoring rule
was changed. During the run we fixed the harness and the run script without changing what is
measured. A response that fills \Q's window is now recorded as context exhaustion, because
llama.cpp signals a full window by stopping the output rather than by rejecting the request. A
padded control runs only after a completed session step, and tool-call arguments that are not
valid JSON are sent back to the model as an empty object. Leakage-check folds are grouped by
image. The pipeline now checks which server profile is loaded and that the vision encoder works
(see Threats to Validity). E2 run~0 is the pilot (same seed and model), so its first six
positions reuse the pilot's cached responses. Two pairs of repair and audit pages turned out to
be identical (B02-V1/V2 and B03-V1/V2), leaving \res{e1-distinct-pages} distinct pages with
\res{e1-distinct-faults} distinct faults. We kept the frozen corpus and also report E1 without
the duplicates. Every page is rechecked after 6\,s, not only pages with timers, which is equal
to or stricter than the plan. After seeing the E2 data we added exploratory counts of tool use
and functional steps per session half, and marked non-functional steps in the drift figure. No public pre-registration tag was created before data collection, so this study
is not pre-registered. The run's code was published (commit \texttt{7544be2}) before all but
a handful of smoke-test calls, which used the same code.

\subsection{RQ1: Capability profiles}
\textbf{Generation (C2, C6).} \res{functional-gen-local-qwen25vl-7b-count} of
\res{functional-gen-local-qwen25vl-7b-n} pages written by \QV{} passed their task's functional
checks. Its nudged generation score was $S_\text{gen} = \res{sgen-local-qwen25vl-7b}$ (95\,\%
CI \res{sgen-local-qwen25vl-7b-ci}), against \res{sgen-unguided-local-qwen25vl-7b} without the
nudge. The default gap of \res{gap-local-qwen25vl-7b} (CI \res{gap-local-qwen25vl-7b-ci}) shows
that the added accessibility sentence made no detectable difference. The share of nudged pages
that passed every applicable check was \res{clean-nudged-local-qwen25vl-7b}, with
\res{vp100-nudged-local-qwen25vl-7b} violating nodes per 100 elements
(\res{vp100-unguided-local-qwen25vl-7b} unguided). Asked whether its page conformed to
WCAG~2.2 AA, the model said yes for a share of \res{overclaim-local-qwen25vl-7b} (CI
\res{overclaim-local-qwen25vl-7b-ci}) of the functional pages that failed at least one check.

\textbf{Repair (C2).} Repair was much harder than generation. \QV{} reached
$S_\text{rep} = \res{srep-local-qwen25vl-7b}$ (CI \res{srep-local-qwen25vl-7b-ci}) and fully
repaired no page (full-repair rate \res{fullrepair-local-qwen25vl-7b}). It often returned the
page as it was:
\res{unchanged-repair-local-qwen25vl-7b-count} of the \res{unchanged-repair-local-qwen25vl-7b-n}
pages it returned were identical to the faulty input. \res{capped-repair-local-qwen25vl-7b-count}
of its \res{capped-repair-local-qwen25vl-7b-n} answers stopped at the 8{,}192-token output cap
before the page was complete. The preservation rate (text and structure kept) was
\res{preserved-local-qwen25vl-7b}. The faults it did resolve were invalid ARIA
attributes (M11, \res{resolve-m11-local-qwen25vl-7b}) and unnamed icon links (M05,
\res{resolve-m05-local-qwen25vl-7b}); it resolved none of the other ten operators. Its score
was \res{srep-w3c-local-qwen25vl-7b} on W3C-derived pages and
\res{srep-authored-local-qwen25vl-7b} on authored pages.

\textbf{Audit (C1).} \QV{} found none of the 192 injected faults (micro-F1
\res{saudit-local-qwen25vl-7b}, recall \res{audit-recall-local-qwen25vl-7b}), and none of the
items it reported matched a fault (precision \res{audit-precision-local-qwen25vl-7b}). Its
near-greedy decoding fell into loops that listed the same element again and again under
consecutive success-criterion numbers. On page B03-V4, for example, it reported one select
element three times under SC 1.4.8, 1.4.9 and 1.4.10, while the page's injected faults were a
missing alt text, low contrast, a missing page language and a demoted heading
(\texttt{runs/e1/scores/audit.jsonl}). \res{capped-audit-local-qwen25vl-7b-count} of its
\res{capped-audit-local-qwen25vl-7b-n} first answers ran into the output cap, and a share of
\res{audit-parsefail-local-qwen25vl-7b} of pages yielded no parseable list even after the JSON
retry.

% ======================================================================================
\section{Threats to Validity}

\textbf{Oracle coverage.} Automated checks find only some WCAG failures, so $a(x)$, the
overclaim rate and audit precision are bounds, not exact values. The probes were validated on
fixtures, not on every possible implementation.

\textbf{Model scale and quantisation.} The models are 4--8B parameters at 4-bit quantisation.
Larger or unquantised models, and other conversions of the same weights, may behave
differently. Results describe these exact files (SHA-256 in the repository).

\textbf{Context window.} \Q{}'s 32{,}768-token window bounds E2: a session ends when its history
no longer fits. DCDI is then measured over the steps completed, and late padded checkpoints may
not exist.

\textbf{The functional gate of DCDI.} DCDI compares adherence only on steps that are functional in
both arms. A session that stops doing the work therefore leaves the comparison instead of
lowering the score, as happened in E2 (Section~\ref{sec:rq2}). The functional checks are also
lenient: they test that the step's anchor element and text exist, so a step whose anchor
already existed passes without any change (the accordion and form-validation steps). DCDI and
$S_5$ must therefore be read together with the functional and tool-use comparison with the
fresh control.

\textbf{Sampling and repetitions.} Provider defaults make \QV{} near-greedy, so its three E1
samples are close to identical. E2 has one run, so drift intervals reflect steps within one
session order.

\textbf{Jury size.} With three families, each E3c pair is judged by one non-recused judge, and
local vision models write and judge alt text less well than larger models. Agreement with BLV
ratings is measured on 68 descriptions.

\textbf{Hardware.} Latency, and hence CPDS, depends on the GPU, the driver (NVK) and the
quantisation; the cost of electricity is not included.

\textbf{Run incidents.} The two \QV{} server profiles (text for E1, vision for E3) share one model
name. The first E3 pass of \QV{} therefore ran against the text-only server, and every one of its
image requests failed. Later, the vision encoder ran out of GPU memory and failed every image
request while the server still reported itself healthy. In both cases the affected steps were
run again on a verified vision server before any result was used. The run script now
checks the loaded profile, warms up the vision encoder, restarts the server on encoder errors and
marks a step done only if none of its requests failed. These incidents explain why
\res{total-calls-failed} of the \res{total-calls} logged call attempts failed. Failed attempts are
never cached or scored.

\textbf{Process.} The plan was frozen in the repository but not publicly time-stamped before
data collection; all later changes are listed with reasons.

% ======================================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
%CONCLUSION-BEGIN
We presented a framework that measures accessible software engineering with browser-based
oracles, a drift index with counterfactual controls, a bias-controlled jury and a cost-aware
efficiency score, and applied it to four models that run for free on one consumer GPU.
%CONCLUSION-END
The harness, prompts, tasks, corpus, call logs and scores are public, so the same study can be
repeated on other hardware or extended to API models by adding keys.

% ======================================================================================
\section*{Artifacts and Reproducibility}
Code, configuration and data are on the \texttt{local-run-2026-11} branch of the project
repository. \texttt{experiments/local/serve\_llamacpp.sh} serves each model with the exact flags
used, \texttt{experiments/local/run\_local.sh} runs the whole study, and
\texttt{experiments/runs/} holds every call record (\texttt{calls.jsonl}), score file and E2
transcript. All tables, figures and values in this paper are regenerated, from \texttt{experiments/}, by
\texttt{python -m analysis.run\_all --paper results/local-run-2026-11} and
\texttt{python local/extra\_values.py}. The study logged \res{total-calls} call attempts
(\res{total-calls-answered} answered) at a total token cost of \res{total-cost}.
